course.title: MongoDB
course.description: A complete practical MongoDB course from BSON and CRUD through workload-driven schema design, aggregation, indexes and query plans, atomicity and transactions, Node.js integration, security, replication, sharding, specialized features, operational readiness, and a final transactional order-service project.
prerequisites: Basic programming concepts: variables, functions, conditions, and object/JSON-like syntax.
Basic HTTP/REST concepts for the application-development modules.
A local MongoDB deployment or MongoDB Atlas/managed environment; advanced topics require the relevant supported deployment.
learningOutcomes: Explain MongoDB's document/BSON model and operate mongosh confidently.
Perform CRUD with precise filters, projections, updates, sorting, bulk writes, and safe cleanup.
Query nested documents and arrays and use expression predicates correctly.
Design schemas from access patterns, growth, relationships, and atomicity needs.
Enforce important structure and value constraints with JSON Schema validation.
Build aggregation pipelines for grouping, joins, array transformations, and time-based analytics.
Design and validate indexes using actual query shapes and explain execution evidence.
Choose between single-document atomicity and multi-document transactions and implement idempotent writes.
Build Node.js services with a reusable MongoClient and error-aware driver code.
Apply authentication, least privilege, TLS, encryption concepts, auditing, and secrets hygiene.
Explain replica-set and sharded-cluster architecture and reason about routing and shard keys.
Use time-series collections, change streams, search/views, monitoring, backups, and restore testing appropriately.
Complete and verify a realistic MongoDB-backed transactional order service.

modules.title: MongoDB Foundations and Tooling
modules.description: Learn the document model, BSON, collections, namespaces, mongosh, and deployment vocabulary.

lessons.title: Documents, Collections, Databases, and BSON
lessons.description: Build the core mental model for MongoDB's document model.
learningObjectives: Explain documents, collections, databases, and namespaces.

notes.text: Document model
MongoDB stores BSON documents in collections. A collection groups related documents without requiring identical field sets. Each document has an _id that uniquely identifies it within the collection.

items: BSON adds types beyond JSON such as ObjectId, Date, Binary, Decimal128, and 64-bit integers.
A BSON document has a 16 MiB size limit.
Flexible schema is a modeling capability, not permission to ignore type consistency or validation.

quiz.question: What is BSON?
options: A binary serialization format used by MongoDB
quiz.answer: A binary serialization format used by MongoDB
quiz.explanation: BSON is MongoDB's binary serialization format and supports additional types.

summary: Build the core mental model for MongoDB's document model. The key capability is to explain documents, collections, databases, and namespaces.

lessons.title: mongosh and Connection Strings
lessons.description: Connect to MongoDB and inspect a learning database.
learningObjectives: Keep credentials out of source code.

notes.text: mongosh is MongoDB's interactive shell. A connection URI describes the target deployment and may contain credentials and topology or TLS options.

mongosh "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017"
use mongo_course_lab
db.getName()
show collections
db.stats()

items: `use` changes the current database context; meaningful database storage appears when data is written.
For hosted deployments, use the connection string provided by the service.
Avoid pasting real passwords into shell history or repositories.

quiz.question: What does `use mongo_course_lab` do?
quiz.answer: Switches the current database context
quiz.explanation: The command changes the active database context in mongosh.

summary: Core takeaway: connect with mongosh.; mongosh and Connection Strings is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: MongoDB CRUD Vocabulary
lessons.description: Map common operations to the core driver and shell methods.
learningObjectives: Distinguish update operators from replacement writes.
Recognize filters and options as separate concerns.

items: Create: insertOne and insertMany.
Read: find, findOne, countDocuments, aggregate.
Update: updateOne, updateMany, replaceOne.
Delete: deleteOne and deleteMany.

notes.text:
db.users.insertOne({name:"Ravi"})
db.users.find({active:true})
db.users.updateOne({name:"Ravi"},{$set:{active:true}})
db.users.deleteOne({name:"Ravi"})

quiz.question: Which operation changes selected fields without replacing the whole document?
quiz.answer: updateOne with update operators
quiz.explanation: Operator-based updates change specified fields while preserving other fields.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on mongodb crud vocabulary, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

lessons.title: Local, Managed, and Production Environments
lessons.description: Choose an environment and isolate configuration.
learningObjectives: Describe local versus managed MongoDB at a high level.
Explain why advanced labs may require replica-set support.

notes.text: A local deployment gives control over the server process and its configuration. A managed service handles many operational concerns. The MongoDB data model is shared, but authentication, networking, backups, monitoring, and feature availability vary by environment.

items: Use local deployments for repeatable low-risk experiments.
Use a managed deployment when you need hosted operations or production-like topology.
Transactions and change streams require a deployment that supports them.

quiz.question: Why keep the MongoDB URI outside application source?
options: Endpoints and credentials are environment-specific and can be sensitive
quiz.answer: Endpoints and credentials are environment-specific and can be sensitive
quiz.explanation: Environment-driven configuration supports safer deployment separation.

summary: The lesson connects MongoDB syntax to an operational decision: describe local versus managed mongodb at a high level.

tasks.title: Build a Reusable MongoDB Lab
tasks.description: Create a scratch database with two collections and verify the connection.
tasks.problemStatement: Create mongo_course_lab with customers and products, insert two documents into each collection, and print counts.
objectives: Verify counts and one sample document.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Exact _id values differ by run because MongoDB generates them.

modules.title: CRUD, Filters, Sorting, and Bulk Writes
modules.description: Develop reliable read/write skills for common application workloads.

lessons.title: Inserts and Ordered Bulk Writes
lessons.description: Create documents efficiently and understand batch failure behavior.

notes.text: db.products.insertMany([{sku:"P1",name:"Keyboard",price:2499},{sku:"P2",name:"Mouse",price:999}],{ordered:false})

items: Bulk insertion reduces repeated client/server calls.
Ordered batches stop after an error; unordered batches can continue with other operations.
Unique indexes enforce identity rules at the database boundary.

quiz.question: What is a key difference between ordered and unordered insertMany?
options: Unordered mode can continue after an individual error
Ordered mode always rolls back the whole batch
quiz.answer: Unordered mode can continue after an individual error
quiz.explanation: Ordered and unordered bulk writes differ in how they proceed after an individual error.

summary: Create documents efficiently and understand batch failure behavior. The key capability is to use insertone and insertmany.

lessons.title: Filters, Projection, and Sorting
lessons.description: Compose precise queries and return only the data the application needs.

notes.text: db.orders.find({status:"paid",total:{$gte:1000,$lt:5000}},{_id:0,total:1,createdAt:1}).sort({createdAt:-1,_id:-1})

items: Implicit top-level fields behave like AND conditions.
Projection reduces response size and can align with covered-query patterns.
Add a unique tie-breaker such as _id when a feed's primary sort field is not unique.

quiz.question: Why add _id as a secondary sort key?
options: To make ordering deterministic when the main sort values tie
quiz.answer: To make ordering deterministic when the main sort values tie
quiz.explanation: A unique tie-breaker prevents ambiguous ordering among equal primary sort values.

summary: Core takeaway: use comparison and logical operators.; Filters, Projection, and Sorting is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Updates, Upserts, and Targeted Deletes
lessons.description: Change only the fields required and clean data safely.

notes.text:
db.inventory.updateOne({sku:"P1",stock:{$gte:1}},{$inc:{stock:-1}})
db.products.updateOne({sku:"P99"},{$set:{name:"New",price:1999}},{upsert:true})
Replacement updates are not the same as operator updates: omitted fields can disappear from a replacement document.

items: Use conditional filters to encode invariants such as non-negative stock.
Use upsert when create-or-update semantics are intentional.
Preview deleteMany filters with find() or countDocuments().

quiz.question: Which operator performs a numeric increment or decrement?
quiz.answer: $inc
quiz.explanation: $inc adjusts a numeric field by a specified amount.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on updates, upserts, and targeted deletes, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

tasks.title: Product CRUD Workflow
tasks.description: Build a repeatable product CRUD script.
tasks.problemStatement: Insert three products, query a price range, update stock, and safely remove a discontinued SKU.
tasks.hint: Run the delete filter as find() first.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The workflow exercises create/read/update/delete with explicit filters and an auditable cleanup step.

modules.title: Nested Documents, Arrays, Expressions, and Cleanup
modules.description: Query complex document shapes and design safe cleanup operations.

lessons.title: Dot Notation for Nested Documents
lessons.description: Query and update fields inside embedded objects.

notes.text:
db.customers.find({"address.city":"Pune"})
db.customers.updateOne({_id:id},{$set:{"address.postalCode":"411001"}})
Dot notation traverses nested object paths. The stored BSON shape must match the path you query; a string cannot be traversed as though it were an object.

items: Nested fields can be indexed.
Embedding can reduce round trips for tightly coupled data.
Validation can constrain nested types and required fields.

quiz.question: How do you query a nested field named city inside address?
quiz.answer: {"address.city":"Pune"}
quiz.explanation: MongoDB uses dot notation for nested object paths.

summary: Query and update fields inside embedded objects. The key capability is to use dotted field paths.

lessons.title: Arrays and $elemMatch
lessons.description: Query array values correctly when multiple conditions must apply to one array element.

notes.text:
db.students.find({scores:{$elemMatch:{subject:"math",score:{$gte:90}}}})
db.orders.updateOne({_id:id},{$addToSet:{tags:"priority"}})

items: $elemMatch correlates multiple predicates to the same array element.
$push appends; $addToSet avoids an exact duplicate; $pull removes matching elements.
Array growth should be bounded when the embedded relationship is expected to grow indefinitely.

quiz.question: When is $elemMatch important?
options: When multiple conditions must match the same array element
quiz.answer: When multiple conditions must match the same array element
quiz.explanation: It makes element-level correlation explicit.

summary: Core takeaway: match scalar arrays.; Arrays and $elemMatch is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: $expr and Field-to-Field Comparisons
lessons.description: Compare document fields using expression evaluation.
learningObjectives: Recognize when derived data may be preferable for hot paths.

notes.text: db.products.find({$expr:{$lt:["$salePrice","$listPrice"]}})
$expr allows aggregation expressions inside a query predicate. It is useful for rules such as salePrice < listPrice or spent > budget.
Computed predicates can be harder to optimize than simple predicates. Validate important workloads with explain() before assuming the performance is adequate.

quiz.question: What does $expr add to a query filter?
quiz.answer: Expression evaluation over document fields
quiz.explanation: $expr evaluates expressions using field values from the document.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on $expr and field-to-field comparisons, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

tasks.title: Cart Array and Expression Queries
tasks.description: Query a cart collection using array and field-comparison semantics.
tasks.problemStatement: Find carts containing a product with quantity >= 2 and identify carts whose total exceeds their budget.
objectives: Use updateMany for a soft-delete/abandonment rule.
tasks.hint: Keep the quantity and SKU predicates inside one $elemMatch.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution demonstrates correlated array matching, field-to-field comparison, and non-destructive cleanup.

modules.title: Workload-Driven Data Modeling and Validation
modules.description: Design document boundaries from access patterns, growth, relationships, and correctness requirements.

lessons.title: Workload-First Schema Design
lessons.description: Start schema design from application operations.

notes.text: Design process
MongoDB schema guidance begins with workload: identify the operations the application performs, then choose document boundaries that make those operations efficient and maintainable.

items: Embed data that is tightly coupled, bounded, and often read together.
Reference data that is shared, independently updated, or high-cardinality.
Keep the BSON document-size limit and growth behavior in mind.

quiz.question: Which case most strongly argues against embedding?
options: Data always read with its parent
quiz.answer: An unbounded child array
quiz.explanation: Unbounded embedded growth can create oversized documents and costly updates.

summary: Start schema design from application operations. The key capability is to list common reads and writes.

lessons.title: Embedding, References, and Historical Snapshots
lessons.description: Choose relationship patterns deliberately.

notes.text: An order may embed a shipping snapshot because the historical address used at checkout is part of the order's meaning. The current customer profile can remain referenced because it has a broader lifecycle.

items: Embedding can support single-document atomicity and fewer round trips.
References suit independently managed or high-cardinality data.
Duplicated data needs an ownership/update policy.

quiz.question: Why might an order store a copy of shipping data?
options: To preserve the historical value used by that order
quiz.answer: To preserve the historical value used by that order
quiz.explanation: Historical transaction records often need the exact values used at the time.

summary: Core takeaway: compare embedding and references.; Embedding, References, and Historical Snapshots is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: JSON Schema Validation
lessons.description: Enforce important document structure at the database boundary.

notes.text: db.createCollection("products",{validator:{$jsonSchema:{bsonType:"object",required:["sku","name","price"],properties:{sku:{bsonType:"string"},name:{bsonType:"string"},price:{bsonType:"number",minimum:0}}}},validationAction:"error"})

items: Database validation protects against malformed writes from multiple clients and tools.
Application validation can provide better user feedback.
Validation does not control user permissions.

quiz.question: What does a collection validator primarily enforce?
quiz.answer: Document shape and value constraints
quiz.explanation: Validators enforce rules on document structure and values.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on json schema validation, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

lessons.title: Schema Evolution and Compatibility
lessons.description: Plan changes while multiple document shapes coexist.
learningObjectives: Use a schema version when useful.

notes.text: {schemaVersion:2,total:1299,currency:"INR"}

items: Additive fields are often easier to roll out than incompatible replacements.
A schemaVersion field can help readers interpret old and new shapes.
Large migrations should be tested and designed for safe retry/resume.

quiz.question: Why can a schemaVersion field be valuable?
options: It lets readers distinguish document shapes during migration
quiz.answer: It lets readers distinguish document shapes during migration
quiz.explanation: Version metadata gives application code an explicit compatibility signal.

summary: The lesson connects MongoDB syntax to an operational decision: use a schema version when useful.

tasks.title: Design and Validate an Order Schema
tasks.description: Create an order collection whose shape reflects its workload and invariants.
tasks.problemStatement: Include customerId, shipping snapshot, status, items, total, and createdAt; validate required fields and types.
objectives: Insert one valid document and show one rejected write.
Query open orders for a customer.
tasks.hint: Keep order-local purchase data together, while independently managed entities may remain referenced.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The validator protects required shape and values while the model keeps transaction-local data together.

modules.title: Aggregation Framework and Analytics
modules.description: Build aggregation pipelines for filtering, grouping, joining, array expansion, and derived reporting.

lessons.title: Pipeline Stages and $match/$project
lessons.description: Process documents through ordered transformation stages.
learningObjectives: Track the shape of documents after each stage.

notes.text: db.orders.aggregate([{$match:{status:"paid"}},{$project:{customerId:1,total:1,createdAt:1,_id:0}}])

items: $match narrows input and may use an index.
$project controls fields flowing to later stages.
Stages such as $unwind and $group can change document cardinality.

quiz.question: Why can an early $match improve a pipeline?
options: It reduces documents processed by later stages and may use an index
quiz.answer: It reduces documents processed by later stages and may use an index
quiz.explanation: Early selective filtering can reduce downstream work.

summary: Process documents through ordered transformation stages. The key capability is to build an ordered pipeline.

lessons.title: $group and Accumulators
lessons.description: Compute grouped business metrics.
learningObjectives: Group by one or more fields.

notes.text: db.sales.aggregate([{$group:{_id:"$category",units:{$sum:"$quantity"},avgPrice:{$avg:"$unitPrice"},minPrice:{$min:"$unitPrice"},maxPrice:{$max:"$unitPrice"}}}])
$sum:1 counts documents; $sum of a field totals that field. Business metrics should be named and defined in terms stakeholders understand.

items: Keep units and currency meanings consistent.
Missing or non-numeric values can change metric behavior; validate the underlying schema.

quiz.question: How can a group count incoming documents?
quiz.answer: $sum:1
quiz.explanation: Each incoming document contributes one to a sum of one.

summary: Core takeaway: use $sum, $avg, $min, and $max.; $group and Accumulators is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: $unwind, $lookup, and Derived Metrics
lessons.description: Expand arrays and join references without double-counting.
learningObjectives: Explain the cardinality change caused by $unwind.

notes.text: db.orders.aggregate([{$unwind:"$items"},{$lookup:{from:"products",localField:"items.sku",foreignField:"sku",as:"product"}},{$set:{product:{$first:"$product"}}}])
If one order has five items, $unwind can produce five pipeline documents. Summing the same order-level total after that step can multiply the total.

items: Join only what the report needs.
Regroup by order when a metric is order-level.
Index common foreign join fields.

practicals.title: Revenue by Customer
practicals.description: Aggregate paid orders into count and revenue per customer.
steps: Match status:'paid'.
Group by customerId.
Calculate count and revenue.
Sort revenue descending.
practicals.output: Each result contains a customer identifier, paid-order count, and revenue.

quiz.question: What does $unwind generally do to an array of N elements?
options: It can produce N pipeline documents from one input document
quiz.answer: It can produce N pipeline documents from one input document
quiz.explanation: $unwind deconstructs an array into separate pipeline documents.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on $unwind, $lookup, and derived metrics, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

tasks.title: Monthly Sales Analytics
tasks.description: Build a monthly category sales report.
tasks.problemStatement: Aggregate paid orders into period, category, units, and revenue.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The pipeline reduces input, expands item arrays, derives line-level revenue, and groups by reporting dimensions.

modules.title: Indexes, Query Planning, and Performance
modules.description: Design indexes from workload patterns and validate them with explain evidence.

lessons.title: Index Purpose and Tradeoffs
lessons.description: Understand why indexes help and what they cost.

notes.text: Indexes provide ordered/searchable structures that can reduce document examination or support sorting. The _id index exists automatically.

items: Index frequent filter and sort paths.
Avoid indexing every field without workload evidence.
Each index has storage and write/update maintenance cost.

quiz.question: What is a normal index tradeoff?
options: It can speed some reads while adding storage and write maintenance
quiz.answer: It can speed some reads while adding storage and write maintenance
quiz.explanation: Indexes trade extra maintenance for faster eligible query paths.

summary: Understand why indexes help and what they cost. The key capability is to explain index-assisted lookup conceptually.

lessons.title: Compound Index Field Order
lessons.description: Design multi-field indexes for actual filter and sort shapes.
learningObjectives: Select an ordered key from a query.

notes.text:
db.orders.createIndex({customerId:1,status:1,createdAt:-1})
db.orders.find({customerId:"C1",status:"paid"}).sort({createdAt:-1})
Compound index order is part of its semantics. `{a:1,b:1}` and `{b:1,a:1}` may support different query shapes.

items: Put fields in an order that matches the workload's equality, range, and sort needs.
Use representative data to confirm the plan.

quiz.question: Why does field order matter in a compound index?
options: It controls which ordered prefixes and query shapes the index can support efficiently
quiz.answer: It controls which ordered prefixes and query shapes the index can support efficiently
quiz.explanation: Compound indexes are ordered key structures, so their prefix matters.

summary: Core takeaway: explain the compound-index prefix concept.; Compound Index Field Order is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Unique, Partial, TTL, and Explain Plans
lessons.description: Enforce uniqueness, lifecycle, and measure query execution.
learningObjectives: Interpret IXSCAN and COLLSCAN at a high level.

notes.text:
db.users.createIndex({email:1},{unique:true})
db.sessions.createIndex({expiresAt:1},{expireAfterSeconds:0})
db.orders.find({customerId:"C1"}).explain("executionStats")

items: A unique index enforces a uniqueness invariant.
A partial index includes only documents matching its filter.
A TTL index is for expiration workflows.
`IXSCAN` commonly indicates index scanning; `COLLSCAN` indicates collection scanning.

practicals.title: Verify an Order Feed Index
practicals.description: Measure a customer/status/date query with explain.
steps: Create the compound index.
Run the find and sort query with explain('executionStats').
Inspect nReturned, totalKeysExamined, totalDocsExamined.
Explain whether the index aligns with the workload.
practicals.output: Explain returns plan and execution statistics; numeric results depend on the dataset.

quiz.question: Which index type supports automatic expiry based on a date field?
quiz.answer: TTL
quiz.explanation: TTL indexes automate expiration based on date/time configuration.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on unique, partial, ttl, and explain plans, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

tasks.title: Explain-Driven Order Feed Optimization
tasks.description: Improve a customer order feed using a compound index and measured plan evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Create and inspect an index supporting customerId/status filters and createdAt descending sort.
tasks.hint: Use the exact filter/sort shape from the application query.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The index mirrors the workload shape; the actual statistics must be read from the explain output.

modules.title: Atomicity, Transactions, Consistency, and Idempotency
modules.description: Choose the smallest correct atomic unit and design failure-aware multi-document workflows.

lessons.title: Single-Document Atomicity
lessons.description: Encode local invariants in one conditional update.
learningObjectives: Use a conditional update for inventory.

notes.text: db.inventory.updateOne({sku:"P1",stock:{$gte:2}},{$inc:{stock:-2}})
A write that changes one document is atomic. A conditional filter can check an invariant at write time, such as stock being sufficient.
Separate documents are not automatically one atomic unit.

quiz.question: What is single-document atomicity?
options: A write to one document is applied atomically with respect to that document
All collections write as one unit
It is equivalent to a backup
quiz.answer: A write to one document is applied atomically with respect to that document
quiz.explanation: MongoDB guarantees atomicity for standard single-document writes.

summary: Encode local invariants in one conditional update. The key capability is to explain document-scope atomicity.

lessons.title: Transactions and Sessions
lessons.description: Group multiple document operations into an atomic business workflow.
learningObjectives: Pass the session to transaction operations.
Explain when a transaction is justified.

notes.text: const s=db.getMongo().startSession();const d=s.getDatabase("shop");s.startTransaction();try{d.orders.insertOne({orderId:"O1"},{session:s});s.commitTransaction()}catch(e){s.abortTransaction();throw e}finally{s.endSession()}

items: Transactions are for business operations spanning multiple documents/collections.
Keep transactions short and focused.
A supported deployment such as an appropriate replica set is required.

quiz.question: When is a transaction most appropriate?
options: When multiple documents must commit or abort as one business operation
quiz.answer: When multiple documents must commit or abort as one business operation
quiz.explanation: Transactions add multi-document atomicity where a single document cannot express the invariant.

summary: Core takeaway: start and end a session.; Transactions and Sessions is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Read/Write Concerns and Idempotency
lessons.description: Choose consistency controls and make retried requests converge safely.
learningObjectives: Distinguish read concern, write concern, and read preference.

notes.text:
db.payments.createIndex({idempotencyKey:1},{unique:true})
db.payments.updateOne({idempotencyKey:"PAY-42"},{$setOnInsert:{orderId:"O1",amount:4999,status:"pending",createdAt:new Date()}},{upsert:true})

items: Read preference chooses eligible members for reads in replicated deployments.
Read concern controls requested read visibility semantics.
Write concern controls write acknowledgement.
Idempotency is a business pattern for safe replay; a unique key enforces identity.

practicals.title: Create an Idempotent Payment
practicals.description: Make duplicate requests converge on one payment.
steps: Create a unique index on idempotencyKey.
Upsert with $setOnInsert.
Repeat the same operation.
Read back the single payment document.
practicals.output: Both attempts target the same unique key; only the first creates the document.

quiz.question: Which setting controls where a replica-set read may be routed?
quiz.answer: readPreference
quiz.explanation: Read preference selects eligible members for reads.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on read/write concerns and idempotency, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

tasks.title: Transactional Checkout
tasks.description: Create an order and reserve inventory atomically.
tasks.problemStatement: Insert an order and decrement two inventory records, aborting when either reservation cannot be made.
objectives: Check matchedCount on each stock update.
Abort on failure and commit on success.
requirements: Replica set or supported managed MongoDB deployment.
tasks.hint: Put the order insert and inventory decrements in the same transaction.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The transaction makes the cross-document checkout atomic.

modules.title: Node.js Application Development
modules.description: Build MongoDB-backed services with the official Node.js driver, reusable connections, transactions, and error handling.

lessons.title: MongoClient Lifecycle
lessons.description: Connect once and reuse the driver client in a long-running service.

items: The driver manages a pool behind MongoClient.
A process should normally reuse one client rather than reconnecting per request.
Connection strings belong in environment or secret configuration.

quiz.question: What is the normal service pattern for MongoClient?
quiz.answer: Reuse one client across requests
quiz.explanation: MongoClient manages pooled connections and is designed for reuse.

summary: Connect once and reuse the driver client in a long-running service. The key capability is to create a mongoclient.

lessons.title: Driver CRUD and Projection
lessons.description: Perform application CRUD and control returned fields.
learningObjectives: Use insertOne, findOne, updateOne, and deleteOne.
Translate common database errors to domain responses.

notes.text: Driver filters are ordinary JavaScript objects. Validate request values before they become database filters, and never treat untrusted input as JavaScript source code.

items: Projection can reduce response payload.
A duplicate-key failure can be mapped to an HTTP 409-style business response.
Keep persistence code behind a service/repository boundary as an application grows.

quiz.question: Which driver method retrieves a single document?
quiz.answer: findOne
quiz.explanation: findOne is the official Node.js driver method for one matching document.

summary: Core takeaway: use insertOne, findOne, updateOne, and deleteOne.; Driver CRUD and Projection is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Transactions in the Node.js Driver
lessons.description: Implement multi-document transactions with sessions.
learningObjectives: Pass the session to every transaction operation.
Use withTransaction or explicit commit/abort semantics.

notes.text: Operations intended to participate in a transaction must use the same session. Avoid unsupported parallel operations within a single transaction.

quiz.question: How does a driver operation join the current transaction?
options: It is given the same session
It is in the same source file
It has the same database name
quiz.answer: It is given the same session
quiz.explanation: The session identifies the transaction context for the operation.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on transactions in the node.js driver, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

lessons.title: Error Handling and Request-Safe Logging
lessons.description: Handle duplicate-key, validation, and operational failures without leaking secrets.
learningObjectives: Log context without credentials or sensitive data.

items: Application errors should expose stable business meaning, not raw stack traces to clients.
Structured logs should include operation context/correlation identifiers but exclude passwords and tokens.
Timeout and retry policy should be designed from workload requirements.

quiz.question: What is MongoDB error code 11000 commonly associated with?
quiz.answer: Duplicate-key violation
quiz.explanation: MongoDB commonly uses code 11000 for duplicate-key errors.

summary: The lesson connects MongoDB syntax to an operational decision: detect common database error conditions.

tasks.title: Node.js Product API
tasks.description: Build a small Express API backed by the official MongoDB driver.
tasks.problemStatement: Implement create/list/update endpoints with a shared MongoClient and unique SKU index.
objectives: Return a conflict on duplicate SKU.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The API separates validation, persistence, uniqueness, and HTTP error translation.

modules.title: MongoDB Security
modules.description: Apply authentication, authorization, TLS, encryption, secrets hygiene, and auditing.

lessons.title: Authentication, Roles, and Least Privilege
lessons.description: Separate identity verification from permissions and minimize application privileges.

items: Authentication verifies identity; authorization governs allowed actions.
Application identities should not normally have administrative privileges.
Separate administrative, application, and monitoring identities where practical.

notes.text: Never commit database passwords, private keys, or connection strings containing secrets to source control.

quiz.question: What does least privilege mean?
options: Grant admin access to every service
quiz.answer: Grant only the permissions required
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits blast radius and accidental misuse.

summary: Separate identity verification from permissions and minimize application privileges. The key capability is to explain authentication versus authorization.

lessons.title: TLS and Network Boundaries
lessons.description: Protect traffic and reduce the reachable attack surface.

items: TLS protects data in transit and supports endpoint authentication when configured correctly.
Network restrictions reduce the systems that can reach the database.
Private networks complement rather than replace encrypted transport.

quiz.question: What does TLS primarily protect?
quiz.answer: Data in transit
quiz.explanation: TLS secures network communication between endpoints.

summary: Core takeaway: explain TLS's purpose.; TLS and Network Boundaries is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Encryption at Rest and Queryable Encryption
lessons.description: Understand storage encryption and encrypted-field query patterns.
learningObjectives: Distinguish encryption at rest from field/query encryption.

notes.text: Encryption at rest protects stored database files and other persisted data from storage-level exposure. Queryable Encryption protects selected fields while retaining defined query capabilities. Exact features and setup vary by deployment and version.

items: Key lifecycle and access controls matter as much as enabling encryption.
Encryption does not replace authentication or authorization.
Protected fields can limit which query/index capabilities are available.

quiz.question: Which threat is encryption at rest primarily designed to reduce?
quiz.answer: Exposure of persisted data
quiz.explanation: Encryption at rest protects stored information against storage-level exposure.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on encryption at rest and queryable encryption, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

lessons.title: Auditing and Secrets Management
lessons.description: Create a practical hardening baseline for a MongoDB deployment.

items: Secrets include passwords, keys, and certificates.
Auditing can capture security-relevant activity in supported deployments/editions.
Hardening also includes restricted network access, dedicated identities, secure file permissions, and protected backups.

quiz.question: Which is a concrete MongoDB hardening measure?
options: Use a dedicated least-privilege application account
Use the DBA account for every service
quiz.answer: Use a dedicated least-privilege application account
quiz.explanation: Separating identities reduces privilege exposure.

summary: The lesson connects MongoDB syntax to an operational decision: identify sensitive configuration.

tasks.title: MongoDB Security Baseline
tasks.description: Create an auditable MongoDB security baseline.
tasks.problemStatement: Cover identities, least privilege, TLS, network restrictions, secrets, encryption, auditing, and backup protection.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The baseline converts broad security principles into reviewable controls while leaving deployment-specific choices explicit.

modules.title: Replication, High Availability, and Sharding
modules.description: Reason about replica sets, read/write routing, sharded components, and shard-key tradeoffs.

lessons.title: Replica Sets and Elections
lessons.description: Understand replication topology and high-availability behavior.
learningObjectives: Describe elections at a high level.

notes.text: A replica set is a group of MongoDB processes that maintain the same data set. One eligible member is normally primary for writes while secondaries replicate data and may become primary after an election.

items: Replica sets provide redundancy and automatic primary election.
Applications should use topology-aware connection strings/drivers rather than pinning themselves to one node.

quiz.question: Which role is normally the write target in a replica set?
quiz.answer: Primary
quiz.explanation: The primary is the normal writable member.

summary: Understand replication topology and high-availability behavior. The key capability is to explain primary/secondary roles.

lessons.title: Read Preference and Write Concern
lessons.description: Choose routing and acknowledgement policies intentionally.

items: Read preference controls eligible members for reads.
Write concern controls acknowledgement requirements for writes.
Secondary reads may reduce pressure on a primary but can return stale data depending on topology and replication lag.

quiz.question: Why might a service read from secondaries?
options: To distribute eligible read workload when its consistency requirements allow it
quiz.answer: To distribute eligible read workload when its consistency requirements allow it
quiz.explanation: Secondary reads are a workload tradeoff.

summary: Core takeaway: explain primary/secondary read preferences.; Read Preference and Write Concern is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Sharded Cluster Components and Shard Keys
lessons.description: Understand mongos, config servers, shards, and distribution keys.
learningObjectives: Differentiate data storage from routing metadata.

notes.text: sh.shardCollection("shop.orders",{customerId:1})

items: mongos routes client operations.
Config servers store sharding metadata.
Shards store application data, normally as replica sets in modern deployments.
Shard keys influence distribution and targeting.

notes.text: A shard key is an architectural commitment. Evaluate cardinality, distribution, access patterns, and hotspot risk before adopting it.

quiz.question: What is mongos?
options: A query router for a sharded cluster
quiz.answer: A query router for a sharded cluster
quiz.explanation: mongos routes operations to relevant shards.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on sharded cluster components and shard keys, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

lessons.title: Targeted Queries, Scatter-Gather, and Hotspots
lessons.description: Evaluate sharding performance from query routing and write distribution.
learningObjectives: Identify hotspot risk from skewed or monotonic keys.
Evaluate a shard-key candidate against queries.

items: Queries that include useful shard-key information can often be targeted.
Queries lacking targeting information may involve multiple shards.
A high-cardinality key can still be a poor choice if access is highly skewed.

quiz.question: Why can a query without a useful shard-key predicate be expensive?
options: It may require work across multiple shards
quiz.answer: It may require work across multiple shards
quiz.explanation: Without targeting information, the router may need to involve multiple shards.

summary: The lesson connects MongoDB syntax to an operational decision: explain targeted versus scatter-gather behavior.

tasks.title: HA and Sharding Architecture Review
tasks.description: Produce an architecture assessment for a growing order service.
tasks.problemStatement: Describe a three-member replica set, application failover expectations, and evaluate a candidate shard key.
tasks.hint: Treat high availability and horizontal distribution as separate decisions.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The plan distinguishes redundancy/election design from scale-out and query-routing design.

modules.title: Specialized MongoDB Features and Production Operations
modules.description: Use time-series, change streams, search/views, monitoring, backup/restore, and readiness practices appropriately.

lessons.title: Time-Series Collections
lessons.description: Model timestamped measurements with MongoDB time-series collections.
learningObjectives: Query measurements over a time interval.

notes.text: db.createCollection("temperature",{timeseries:{timeField:"timestamp",metaField:"sensorId",granularity:"minutes"}})
Time-series collections are designed for sequences of measurements recorded over time. `timeField` records measurement time; `metaField` can identify a series or shared metadata.

items: Choose granularity based on expected measurement frequency.
Time-bounded queries are a natural workload.
Verify feature support before assuming every normal-collection capability applies.

quiz.question: Which field is required in a time-series collection definition?
quiz.answer: timeField
quiz.explanation: MongoDB requires a timeField for time-series collections.

summary: Model timestamped measurements with MongoDB time-series collections. The key capability is to create a time-series collection.

lessons.title: Change Streams and Event-Driven Data Flows
lessons.description: React to database changes without polling.

notes.text:
const stream=db.orders.watch();
stream.on("change",change=>console.log(change.operationType,change.documentKey));
Change streams expose data changes from supported replica-set and sharded deployments. The change event has an identifier/resume token that can support restarting from a prior position.
MongoDB documentation notes collection-specific feature restrictions; current docs state time-series collections do not support change streams.

quiz.question: What is a common use for change streams?
options: Trigger downstream workflows after database changes
quiz.answer: Trigger downstream workflows after database changes
quiz.explanation: Change streams provide application-visible database change events.

summary: Core takeaway: open a change stream.; Change Streams and Event-Driven Data Flows is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Search, Views, and Capped Collections
lessons.description: Select specialized features based on the retrieval/storage problem.
learningObjectives: Distinguish ordinary indexes from Atlas Search.

items: Atlas Search addresses richer text retrieval; Atlas Vector Search addresses similarity retrieval use cases.
Views provide logical queryable representations of source collections.
Capped collections have fixed size and are suited to specific append-oriented patterns.

quiz.question: What is a MongoDB view?
options: A logical queryable representation derived from source data
quiz.answer: A logical queryable representation derived from source data
quiz.explanation: A view exposes a defined read representation without being an independent duplicate dataset.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on search, views, and capped collections, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

lessons.title: Testing MongoDB-Backed Applications
lessons.description: Validate persistence logic with isolated data and deterministic assertions.
learningObjectives: Separate integration tests from pure unit tests.
Use isolated test databases or collections.
Assert database state rather than incidental console output.

items: Unit tests should cover business logic that does not require MongoDB.
Integration tests should exercise real driver calls against an isolated MongoDB environment.
Seed fixtures deliberately and clean them between tests or use isolated namespaces/databases.
Test duplicate-key, validation, not-found, transaction-abort, and retry/idempotency paths—not only happy paths.

quiz.question: What should an integration test for a MongoDB service primarily verify?
options: Observed persistence behavior and business invariants
Only the text of a console log
quiz.answer: Observed persistence behavior and business invariants
quiz.explanation: Integration tests should verify the database-backed behavior that unit tests cannot prove.

summary: Students apply testing mongodb-backed applications directly in MongoDB practice.

lessons.title: Current Practices vs Legacy MongoDB Features
lessons.description: Recognize supported modern workflows and clearly label deprecated or legacy approaches.
learningObjectives: Distinguish mongosh from the legacy mongo shell.
Explain that map-reduce is deprecated in modern MongoDB and aggregation is the preferred framework.
Treat version-sensitive features as documentation checks.

notes.text: MongoDB's current tooling and documentation should be the default reference for new work. The legacy `mongo` shell has been superseded by `mongosh`, and map-reduce is deprecated in modern MongoDB; aggregation pipelines provide the contemporary analytics model.

items: Do not teach deprecated tooling as the default workflow.
When maintaining legacy systems, understand the old feature well enough to migrate safely.
Version-sensitive behavior must be checked against the MongoDB version deployed.

quiz.question: What is the preferred modern approach for analytics that historically used map-reduce?
quiz.answer: Aggregation pipelines
quiz.explanation: MongoDB deprecated map-reduce in favor of aggregation pipelines for supported analytics workloads.

summary: Students apply current practices vs legacy mongodb features directly in MongoDB practice.

tasks.title: Operations Runbook
tasks.description: Write an evidence-driven runbook for a MongoDB-backed service.
tasks.problemStatement: Cover slow queries, duplicate-key errors, restore, failover, and credential rotation.
tasks.hint: Start with observation and evidence before mutating production data.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The runbook emphasizes evidence, controlled action, and verification.

modules.title: Final Real-World Project — Transactional Order Service
modules.description: Integrate MongoDB modeling, indexing, validation, transactions, Node.js, change streams, and operational verification.

lessons.title: Project Architecture and Data Model
lessons.description: Design the service boundary and MongoDB collections.
learningObjectives: Choose embedded order data and referenced inventory.

items: Collections: products, inventory, orders, orderAudit.
Embedded order items preserve purchase-time unit prices and quantities.
Inventory is separate because stock is shared across orders.
Unique indexes protect SKU and idempotency identity.
Checkout uses a transaction because it spans multiple documents.

notes.text:
Client -> Express -> MongoClient -> MongoDB
                         |-> products
                         |-> inventory
                         |-> orders
                         |-> orderAudit

quiz.question: Which project action most clearly needs a transaction?
options: Create an order and decrement multiple inventory documents
quiz.answer: Create an order and decrement multiple inventory documents
quiz.explanation: The checkout workflow must commit or abort several document changes together.

summary: Design the service boundary and MongoDB collections. The key capability is to map service components.

lessons.title: Project Correctness Controls
lessons.description: Combine validation, uniqueness, idempotency, and conditional stock updates.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of an idempotency key.

items: The project represents money as integer minor units for simple lab arithmetic.
A production financial application should choose and document a precision representation suitable for its requirements.
The database should enforce invariants that must hold under concurrency.

quiz.question: Which combination best protects checkout from replay and overselling?
options: Unique idempotency key, transaction, and conditional stock update
quiz.answer: Unique idempotency key, transaction, and conditional stock update
quiz.explanation: These controls address request replay, cross-document atomicity, and inventory conditions.

summary: Core takeaway: use unique indexes for identities.; Project Correctness Controls is reinforced with the accompanying MongoDB examples.

lessons.title: Project Execution and Verification
lessons.description: Run the service and validate its observable behavior.
learningObjectives: Verify inventory changes once under a repeated idempotency key.
Inspect audit events and index behavior.

items: The complete source is embedded under `project.files`; the physical ZIP intentionally contains only course.json.
The project needs a deployment that supports transactions and change streams.
Exact generated IDs and response bodies vary by run.

notes.text:
npm install
npm run seed
npm start
./test/checkout.sh

quiz.question: What should happen when the same idempotency key is submitted twice?
options: The same logical order is returned and inventory is not reserved twice
quiz.answer: The same logical order is returned and inventory is not reserved twice
quiz.explanation: Idempotency makes repeated delivery converge on one logical operation.

summary: Students leave this lesson with a practical handle on project execution and verification, plus the decision points needed in the next module.

project.name: Transactional Order Service
project.description: A Node.js/Express service that creates idempotent orders, reserves inventory transactionally, serves products and orders, checks database health, and records order changes through a change-stream audit projection.
steps: Use a local replica set or supported managed deployment for transactions and change streams.
Reconstruct the project files from `project.files` in this course JSON.
Run npm install and set MONGODB_URI, MONGODB_DB, and PORT through the environment.
Run npm run seed, then npm start.
Verify GET /health and GET /products.
Run test/checkout.sh and observe order creation and inventory reservation.
Repeat the same checkout request with the same idempotency key and verify that inventory decreases only once.
Inspect orderAudit to confirm change-stream events are projected.
Use explain() on the customerId/createdAt order query and inspect the supporting index.
Before production deployment, add authentication/authorization, TLS, structured logs, robust automated tests, secret management, backups, restore drills, and deployment-specific monitoring.

files.test/checkout.sh:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
BASE_URL="${BASE_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:3000}"
KEY="demo-$(date +%s)"

curl -fsS "$BASE_URL/health"; echo
curl -fsS "$BASE_URL/products"; echo

payload=$(cat <<JSON
{"customerId":"C-100","idempotencyKey":"$KEY","items":[{"sku":"KB-01","quantity":1},{"sku":"MS-01","quantity":2}]}
JSON
)

curl -fsS -X POST "$BASE_URL/orders" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$payload"; echo
curl -fsS -X POST "$BASE_URL/orders" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$payload"; echo

project.explanation: The service keeps order-local purchase state in an embedded order document while inventory remains a separate collection because stock is shared across orders. Checkout is the multi-document atomic boundary: it resolves prices, conditionally decrements inventory, and inserts the order under one transaction. A unique idempotencyKey index makes retries converge. The reusable MongoClient manages pooled connections, and a change stream creates a simple audit projection. The project is a learning baseline rather than a turnkey production system; production work should add authentication/authorization, TLS, strong secret handling, structured observability, automated tests, and a documented monetary-precision policy.
